title: Strategic asset allocation
decision_question: Does the written mix of asset classes still match the horizon, risk capacity and contribution policy, or is no change warranted?
required_portfolio_data: Current weights for each class named in the written policy ;; Written target weights, or an explicit record that targets are not set ;; Standing contribution amount, currency and frequency ;; Balances the policy treats as investable, and balances it keeps outside that mix
required_market_or_economic_data: None. A return forecast is not required.
investor_policy_constraints: The written policy is the anchor ;; Balances the policy excludes stay outside the investable mix ;; A missing target stays missing and is not replaced with a default mix ;; No order is produced
evidence: Harry Markowitz; 1952; Portfolio Selection; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x || Gary P. Brinson, L. Randolph Hood and Gilbert L. Beebower; 1986; Determinants of Portfolio Performance; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v42.n4.39 || Roger G. Ibbotson and Paul D. Kaplan; 2000; Does Asset Allocation Policy Explain 40, 90, or 100 Percent of Performance?; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v56.n1.2327
evidence_limitations: Markowitz (1952) is a framework for choosing a mix from expected returns, risks and correlations. It does not supply those inputs, and estimated inputs are uncertain. ;; Brinson, Hood and Beebower (1986) is often misread as proof that policy explains performance. Their study describes the variation of returns over time for a sample of large US pension plans. It is not proof that a policy mix outperforms. ;; Ibbotson and Kaplan (2000) show that the share linked to policy depends on which question is asked: variation over time, differences across funds, or the level of return. Their samples are not this portfolio, and the paper is not a forecast. ;; Institutional use is not proof of outperformance.
applicable_conditions: The horizon is long enough that the decision is the strategic mix rather than a known cash need ;; The policy names the balances in scope, or the review records that it does not
contradictory_conditions: The same decision is being used to time a region, sector or market ;; Target weights would be invented because none were written ;; A short-term spending need is being rewritten as a strategic weight
implementation_alternatives: No action. ;; Continue the existing contribution policy. ;; Record that targets are not set and stop ;; Record that any change to the written mix needs a separate human decision, and stop
expected_trade_offs: A broader mix can reduce reliance on one class and can also dilute a concentrated position the policy wanted ;; Changing the written mix resets the anchor, so it should be uncommon ;; Leaving the mix unchanged avoids turnover and leaves drift to be handled, if at all, by later contributions
outcome_evaluation_criteria: The recorded decision names the written policy that was in force ;; Contributions are kept separate from investment return ;; No numerical efficacy rank is recorded. ;; A later review can say whether the mix was left unchanged, held for a separate human decision, or blocked because targets were missing

title: Diversification across regions and sectors
decision_question: Do the current holdings spread exposure across regions and sectors in line with the written policy, or is any concentration accepted in that policy?
required_portfolio_data: Regional weights of holdings in scope, where a holdings source supports them ;; Sector weights of holdings in scope, where a holdings source supports them ;; Any region, sector or single-holding limit written in the policy ;; An explicit gap where look-through holdings are not available from a cited source
required_market_or_economic_data: None. A return forecast is not required. ;; A forecast of future correlations is not an input
investor_policy_constraints: Concentration limits written in the policy are the limits that apply ;; Regions or sectors the policy excludes stay excluded ;; A missing holdings breakdown is a gap and is not stored as a zero weight ;; No order is produced
evidence: Harry Markowitz; 1952; Portfolio Selection; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x || Bruno H. Solnik; 1974; Why Not Diversify Internationally Rather Than Domestically?; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v30.n4.48 || François Longin and Bruno Solnik; 2001; Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets; https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00340
evidence_limitations: Markowitz (1952) shows why imperfect correlation can reduce portfolio variance. It does not say that every regional or sector split is useful, and it does not estimate today's correlations. ;; Solnik (1974) reports risk reduction from adding foreign equities in the markets and period he studied. Costs, taxes and later correlation regimes sit outside that result. ;; Longin and Solnik (2001) find that correlation across international equity markets rises in bear markets, so the spread of losses can narrow when a decline is already under way. They do not find the same rise in bull markets. Sector labels can still hide a shared economic exposure. ;; Institutional use is not proof of outperformance.
applicable_conditions: Holdings can be classified from a cited source, or the missing classification is shown ;; The review describes the written policy rather than forecasting which region or sector will lead
contradictory_conditions: Weights would be filled in without a holdings source ;; A change would rotate into a region or sector because of a predicted return ;; A known future need in one currency is ignored
implementation_alternatives: No action. ;; Continue the existing contribution policy. ;; Record an unclassified or concentrated holding as a stated gap ;; Record that any change to holdings needs a separate human decision, and stop
expected_trade_offs: More regions and sectors can reduce single-market exposure and can add cost, tax and tracking complexity ;; One broad holding can spread risk more honestly than several overlapping sector holdings ;; Concentration that the policy accepts should stay visible
outcome_evaluation_criteria: The review lists the weights that were known and the weights that were missing ;; No correlation forecast is presented as a fact ;; Regions and sectors are not ranked by expected return ;; No numerical efficacy rank is recorded. ;; Continuing the contribution policy counts as a completed outcome

title: Contribution-based rebalancing
decision_question: Should the next contribution, if one is due under the existing policy, be directed towards underweight classes in the written mix, or should that contribution policy continue unchanged?
required_portfolio_data: Current weights and the written target weights ;; Standing contribution amount, currency and frequency ;; Whether a contribution is actually due ;; Dealing, tax and income constraints the policy has already recorded
required_market_or_economic_data: None. A return forecast is not required. ;; Prices are used only to state current weights
investor_policy_constraints: The contribution stays within the written amount and frequency ;; Underweight is measured against the written targets, not against a forecast ;; If targets are missing, the contribution has no invented destination ;; A sale is not required ;; No order is produced
evidence: André F. Perold and William F. Sharpe; 1988; Dynamic Strategies for Asset Allocation; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v44.n1.16 || Colleen M. Jaconetti, Francis M. Kinniry Jr. and Yan Zilbering; 2010; Best practices for portfolio rebalancing; Vanguard research, July 2010
evidence_limitations: Perold and Sharpe (1988) compare buy-and-hold, constant-mix and portfolio-insurance rules. Buy-and-hold is a do-nothing strategy. Constant-mix buys after falls and sells after rises. In their framework, constant-mix does better when markets are trendless and volatile, and worse when markets trend. They do not test directing new contributions only, and they do not rank the rules by a single score. ;; Jaconetti, Kinniry and Zilbering (2010), in Vanguard research on US stock and bond data, report no single optimal rebalancing frequency or threshold in that study. They describe the aim as staying near a target rather than maximising return. The note does not test contribution-only rebalancing, and no threshold or calendar from that note is adopted here. The note cites earlier policy-attribution studies, which are often misread as proof that policy explains performance. ;; Institutional use is not proof of outperformance.
applicable_conditions: A contribution is due under the existing policy, or the review confirms that none is due ;; Written target weights exist, or their absence is the reason to stop
contradictory_conditions: The contribution would be timed because a market is expected to rise or fall ;; Targets would be invented in order to give the contribution a destination ;; The playbook is treated as a reason to sell an overweight holding
implementation_alternatives: No action. ;; Continue the existing contribution policy. ;; Note that the next due contribution could be directed towards underweight classes named in the written policy, for a later human decision, without a sale and without an order ;; Record that targets or the contribution amount are missing and stop
expected_trade_offs: Using new money can move weights towards the written mix with fewer sales than a full rebalance ;; When contributions are small relative to the portfolio, the gap to target closes slowly ;; In a trending market, moving back towards target weights can lag a mix that is left unchanged ;; Perold and Sharpe describe that trade-off for constant-mix rules. They do not price it for this portfolio
outcome_evaluation_criteria: The review states whether a contribution was due and whether targets existed ;; It records no action, an unchanged contribution policy, or a direction held for a later human decision ;; It does not record a sale or an order ;; No numerical efficacy rank is recorded.

title: Cost and tracking efficiency
decision_question: Are the cited ongoing charges, and any cited tracking difference, consistent with the written policy, or is a figure missing so that the comparison stops?
required_portfolio_data: Ongoing charge for each holding in scope, from a cited document ;; Tracking difference only where a cited document states it ;; Any maximum ongoing charge written in the policy ;; Domicile, currency and accumulating or distributing treatment already recorded for the holding
required_market_or_economic_data: None. A return forecast is not required. ;; A benchmark total return is not invented to fill a gap
investor_policy_constraints: Compare the same share class, currency and cost basis ;; A missing charge is a gap and is not stored as zero ;; The lowest charge is not selected automatically ;; No order is produced
evidence: William F. Sharpe; 1991; The Arithmetic of Active Management; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v47.n1.7 || William F. Sharpe; 2013; The Arithmetic of Investment Expenses; https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v69.n2.2 || Mark M. Carhart; 1997; On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03808.x || Kenneth R. French; 2008; Presidential Address: The Cost of Active Investing; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01368.x
evidence_limitations: Sharpe (1991) is an argument about the average actively managed unit before and after costs. It is not a result for every fund, and it is not a forecast. ;; Sharpe (2013) sets out how expense differences can change terminal wealth under stated assumptions. Those illustrations are not an expected result for this portfolio. ;; Carhart (1997) studies US equity mutual funds from 1962 to 1993. Expenses and transaction costs explain much of the persistence he finds. That sample does not measure a current holding. ;; French (2008) estimates the cost of active investing in the US stock market from 1980 to 2006. The estimate is not a saving this register promises. ;; An ongoing charge is not a tracking difference. Sampling, securities lending, withholding tax and foreign exchange can matter as much as the fee. No figure is filled in when the source is missing. ;; Institutional use is not proof of outperformance.
applicable_conditions: At least one cited ongoing charge is available, or the review stops at the gap ;; The policy states a cost limit, or the review is descriptive only
contradictory_conditions: A higher charge would be accepted because the holding is expected to beat the market by enough to cover it ;; Charges would be compared across currencies or share classes without saying so ;; Tracking difference would be assumed equal to the ongoing charge
implementation_alternatives: No action. ;; Continue the existing contribution policy. ;; Record each missing ongoing charge or tracking figure and stop ;; Leave the cited cost comparison for a later human decision, with no order
expected_trade_offs: A lower ongoing charge can leave more of the market result and can come with a wider spread, thinner liquidity or a less suitable domicile ;; Close tracking of a benchmark the policy did not choose is not itself a reason to hold it ;; Changing holdings to save a small charge can cost more in tax and spread than the charge that is saved
outcome_evaluation_criteria: The review lists the cited charges and the missing ones ;; A fee gap is not converted into an expected-return rank ;; A low charge is not recorded as outperformance ;; No numerical efficacy rank is recorded. ;; No action remains a recorded outcome

title: Tactical regional or sector allocation
decision_question: Should a region or sector be overweighted or underweighted because of a predicted relative return? While this entry is not approved, the answer is to leave the strategic mix unchanged.
required_portfolio_data: Current regional and sector weights ;; The written strategic weights that a tilt would leave ;; Costs of changing the mix, where those costs are already known
required_market_or_economic_data: A timing rule would need a point-in-time forecast of regional or sector relative returns, with a source and a vintage ;; That forecast is not an authorised input while this entry is not approved
investor_policy_constraints: The written strategic policy remains the anchor ;; This entry must not be applied ;; No order is produced ;; Institutional use of a tactical product is not a reason to apply one
evidence: Robert C. Merton; 1981; On Market Timing and Investment Performance. I. An Equilibrium Theory of Value for Market Forecasts; https://doi.org/10.1086/296137 || Ivo Welch and Amit Goyal; 2008; A Comprehensive Look at The Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction; https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhm014
evidence_limitations: Merton (1981) sets out the value of a market-timing forecast. It is a hurdle for a forecast, and it is not evidence that a regional or sector forecast clears that hurdle. ;; Welch and Goyal (2008) review predictors of the equity premium and find poor and unstable performance, in sample and out of sample, over the years they studied. Their tests are not a direct test of a regional or sector rotation rule, so the result does not by itself approve or reject a named tilt. ;; Published timing results can look stronger in sample than out of sample. That contest is unresolved, which is why this entry is not approved. ;; Institutional use is not proof of outperformance.
applicable_conditions: The entry may be read as research so a later review can see why a timing change was refused ;; No condition on this version authorises a change to the portfolio
contradictory_conditions: Any change to weights, contributions or orders based on a predicted regional or sector return ;; Treating a backtest, a house view or institutional practice as approval ;; Treating this entry as a structural principle
implementation_alternatives: No action. ;; Continue the existing contribution policy. ;; Keep the written strategic mix ;; Record the timing idea as not approved and stop
expected_trade_offs: A tilt that later proves right can differ from the strategic mix, and a tilt that proves wrong can differ in the other direction. The sign is not known in advance ;; Trading a tilt adds cost and departs from the written policy ;; Refusing the tilt keeps the policy and the contribution rule intact
outcome_evaluation_criteria: Confirm this entry was not applied ;; Confirm no order was suggested ;; Confirm the strategic mix and the existing contribution policy were left as they were ;; Do not score the forecast that was refused ;; No numerical efficacy rank is recorded.
